newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Florida faces tough choice on sugar tax.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Florida faces tough choice on sugar tax.

text.p: In the row over Florida sugar, the only certainty is that the once-pristine waters of the Everglades need help.

On election day on November 5, Florida voters will be asked to enshrine in the state constitution a penny-a-pound tax on raw sugar grown in the Everglades with the proceeds -- an estimated $900 million over 25 years -- used to clean up the priceless River of Grass.

The sugar tax proposal has brought to a boil a decades-old battle between farmers and ecologists over fertiliser pollution of the unique Everglades, a refuge for endangered species and prime source of drinking water for millions of Florida citizens.

Muddling a confusing issue is the source of financing for the environmentalists' pro-tax side: wealthy Wall Street commodities trader Paul Tudor Jones, who has taken millions of dollars from his own pocket to fuel the fight for the tax.
Campaign spending, at last count more than $27 million, has made it a sweet issue for TV and radio stations and one of the most expensive ballot drives in American history.
"These are not poor farmers," says Mary Barley, chairwoman of the Save Our Everglades group that champions the initiative. "All we're asking is that they pay their fair share."

"It's being put in the constitution. Right next to freedom of speech and freedom of religion, it will now say "thou shalt have a tax,'" counters Robert Buker of the U.S. Sugar Corp. "The constitution isn't the place for this kind of thing."
The choice is a complicated one for Florida voters, who are known to love their environment and hate new taxes.

In a Mason-Dixon Florida Poll conducted on October 11-13, the "yes" vote led 49-40 percent with 11 percent undecided. But pollster Robert Joffee said the results signalled a good chance the initiative would be defeated because undecided voters usually cast "no" ballots on tax questions.
HEART OF THE SUGAR INDUSTRY
In vast fields fanning out from tiny Clewiston, the sugar cane rises 10 feet (3.5 metres) high from the rich black soil that makes this the heart of the U.S. sugar industry.

The sign at the edge of Clewiston, population 6,000, reads "America's Sweetest Town." U.S. 27 becomes the "Sugarland Highway" where it rolls in from the green fields. Even the football stadium -- Cane Field -- reflects the local flavour.

"Sugar makes this town," said Mickey Acree, who grew up near the cane fields bordering Lake Okeechobee. Like many locals, Acree is a vigorous opponent of the tax. "Vote No to Sugar Tax" reads the sign outside his Kentucky Fried Chicken shop, across the street from the Sugar Corp's headquarters.
"People say a penny a pound and it don't seem like much, but when you look at the total tonnage...that's a big old chunk of money," he said. "I'm scared. It's going to hurt."
TAX WILL KILL US - GROWERS SAY

Florida growers -- dubbed "Big Sugar" by environmentalists -- harvested 417,000 acres (168,800 hectares) last year and produced 14.5 million tonnes of sugar worth $485.3 million, more than half the value of all U.S.-produced sugar, according to state statistics.

The industry is dominated by the giants, the U.S. Sugar Corp, an employee-owned company started in 1928, and Flo-Sun, owned by brothers Alfonso and Jose Fanjul, wealthy immigrants whose family grew sugar in Cuba before Fidel Castro's revolution.
The growers say a sugar tax will kill the industry. "We think the entire sugar industry will go out of business over the course of years. It will strangle to death," said Buker.

Tax advocates say growers, protected by a U.S. programme that limits sugar imports, can well afford it. "This is so lucrative, they are not going to be driven out," said Barley. "Under the farm programme, they are guaranteed a profit."
John Mengel, head of the sugar analysis group with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), said the claim that sugar farmers are guaranteed profits through government subsidies is wrong.
"We adjust supplies to demand, which results in a certain price," he said. "We don't write cheques to growers."
Tax advocates say the farmers make five cents a pound on sugar. Growers say their profit is less than a penny a pound.

A USDA study indicated the Florida crop last year netted about half-a-cent per pound on average, but officials concede that the biggest growers, who also process sugar, do not need a profit on the harvest because refining is so lucrative.

U.S. Sugar, which produced 650,000 tonnes of sugar last year, is a private company and refuses to reveal how much it makes. But Buker argues the point is moot. "The answer to this isn't 'tell me how much you make and I'll take it,'" he said.
CAMPAIGN IS AMONG COSTLIEST IN U.S. HISTORY

As of last week, the two sides had spent nearly $27 million to win votes, making the sugar initiative the most expensive in Florida history and the second-costliest in U.S. history, behind only a California referendum on no-fault insurance.
The figure included about $17 million spent by the growers and $10 million by the pro-tax campaign. Jones has supplied about 85 percent of the money in the pro-tax coffers, according to Barley.

"Whatever his reasons are, it's not because he's an environmentalist. I think it's because he stands to make a lot of money off of it," said Buker, adding that the industry will spend whatever it takes to win. "This is a death sentence for us so we are going to spend every dime we can borrow."

Jones, who was unavailable for comment, was sued by U.S. Sugar earlier this year for allegedly trying to direct excess contributions to Richard Lugar, chairman of the Senate Committee on Agriculture and an opponent of sugar subsidies.

Campaign advertising has been criticised as misleading. One anti-tax ad barely mentions the Everglades and portrays the initiative as a tax grab by bureaucrats who would only spend it wastefully. In fact, a petition landed the issue on the ballot and the tax would be paid by farmers, not consumers.

"I don't think the sides are distorting the truth as much as they are shading the facts," said Tim Lenz, political science professor of Florida Atlantic University. "If the growers talk about polluting the Everglades, they lose. So they change the terms of the debate."

Lenz said the intrigue in the debate is that growers, for the first time, have been pushed from the comfort of Capitol Hill into the public arena, where their fate will be decided by voters, not politicians susceptible to powerful lobbies.
"For years agriculture interests were able to prevail in legislative policy setting," he said. "When you take farm policy out of that setting, the balance of power tips."
ECOSYSTEM IN THE BALANCE

What no one disputes is that the Everglades, a river of sluggish water and razor-sharp sawgrass inhabited by the endangered Florida panther, alligator, deer and myriad species of birds and insects, is ailing -- polluted by over-development on its flanks and poisoned by years of chemical runoff from farms within and to the north.

For years, the more strident of environmentalists have said that sugar farming is incompatible with the Everglades. Tax advocates insist this campaign is not out to drive the growers off the land. But, says Barley, "obviously water is more important than sugar."

The growers ask "If not here, where?" Would it be better for Brazil to hack down rainforest to grow more sugar in order to fill the void if Florida growers go down? And what becomes of the Everglades farmland?
"If they tax sugar, we'll just put condos (condominium) up," said Buker. "Now are condos going to be better for the Everglades than sugar? I think not."
